title: Climbing Kilimanjaro: Full Guide
excerpt: Kilimanjaro, 5,895 m, is the highest mountain in Africa. The full guide: the Machame Route day by day, summit night, acclimatisation, seasons, fees and costs.
seoTitle: Climbing Kilimanjaro: Machame Route Guide, Costs and Seasons

content.value: At midnight, at Barafu Camp at 4,673 m, the headlamps come on and a long line of lights begins to climb through the dark towards Uhuru Peak. Climbing Kilimanjaro, 5,895 m, the highest mountain in Africa, requires no technical climbing experience: on the Machame Route, which we climb, it is a journey of seven days on the mountain within a 9-day expedition, with nights in tents, a long summit night and gradual acclimatisation. What it does require is good fitness, warm gear and patience. The recommended seasons are January to February and June to October.

For many people Kilimanjaro is the first high mountain of their lives, so it also raises the most questions: which route to choose, how many days you really need, what happens on summit night, how hard the altitude is and what the price includes. This guide answers them one by one, based on the expedition we run on the mountain, day by day. If you dream of standing on the roof of Africa, this is where to start.
What Kilimanjaro actually is

Kilimanjaro rises in northern Tanzania, close to the border with Kenya. It is the highest mountain on the African continent and one of the Seven Summits, the highest points on each continent. It is not part of a mountain range but a solitary volcano rising from the plain, made up of three volcanic cones: Shira, Mawenzi and Kibo. Uhuru Peak, 5,895 m, is the highest point on the crater rim of Kibo.

What makes the climb special is the passage between climate zones. In seven days you cross five different zones: cultivated land at the foot of the mountain, rainforest, a zone of shrubs and tall grasses, alpine desert, and finally the frozen summit zone, with snow and glaciers. The whole mountain lies within Kilimanjaro National Park, and a foreign climber may only climb it through a licensed company and with a local guide.
Why the Machame Route

Kilimanjaro has several ascent routes. The Marangu Route is the only one where you sleep in huts, and the other routes, among them Lemosho, Rongai and Umbwe, are camping routes. Machame climbs from the south-western side of the mountain, crosses the Shira Plateau, circles the summit cone from the south and reaches Barafu Camp, from where you set out for the summit. The descent follows a different trail, via Mweka Camp, so you hardly ever retrace your steps.

We chose Machame because of its profile. On the fourth day of the expedition you climb to the Lava Tower, 4,600 m, and descend to sleep at Barranco Camp, 3,900 m. This is the principle of "climb high, sleep low", and it lets the body meet the altitude before summit night. Seven days on the mountain give the body time to acclimatise gradually, and the scenery changes almost every day, from the rainforest to the snow near the summit.

content.value: Our route, day by day
This is how the HighAir Kilimanjaro expedition is built. The altitudes in brackets are those of the night stop or of the highest point that day:

items: Day 1: landing at Kilimanjaro International Airport, a drive of about an hour to the hotel in Moshi, gear check and briefing with the guide team.
Day 2: a drive of about an hour to Machame Gate (1,800 m) and a walk through the rainforest to Machame Camp (2,835 m). 11 km, 5 to 7 hours.
Day 3: out of the rainforest to Shira Camp (3,750 m). 5 km, 4 to 6 hours.
Day 4: ascent to the Lava Tower (4,600 m) and descent to sleep at Barranco Camp (3,900 m). 10 km, 6 to 8 hours.
Day 5: climbing the Barranco Wall (4,200 m) and descent to Karanga Camp (3,995 m). 6 km, 4 to 6 hours.
Day 6: a short ascent to Barafu Camp (4,673 m) and rest before the midnight start. 4 km, 4 to 5 hours.
Day 7: summit night, ascent to Uhuru Peak (5,895 m) and descent to Mweka Camp (3,100 m). 17 km, 13 to 15 hours.
Day 8: descent to Mweka Gate (1,640 m), a festive lunch with the crew and back to the hotel in Moshi. 8 km, 3 to 4 hours.
Day 9: transfer to the airport and flight home, or on to the safari.

content.value: In total you walk about 61 km on the mountain. Most days are not especially long, and the difficulty is concentrated on day 7. Before leaving camp the guides carry out a routine medical check, and on the Barranco Wall there are sections where you climb using hands and feet, on a narrow path and at a slow pace.

content.title: ✦ Climb high, sleep low
content.value: On day 4 you climb to the Lava Tower, a 90 m volcanic rock formation whose top stands at 4,600 m, and descend to sleep 700 metres lower, at Barranco Camp. Climbing to altitude and sleeping lower speeds up acclimatisation, and this is the most important preparation day for summit night.
Summit night

Day 6 is the shortest walking day of the climb. You reach Barafu Camp, 4,673 m, have lunch and go to rest early. The wake-up call is at midnight: you put on every layer of clothing, switch on your headlamp and set off.

The ascent to the summit takes about eight hours, at a very slow pace and with short breaks for rest and drinking. The trail climbs a steep scree slope to Stella Point, on the crater rim of Kibo, and from there you continue along the rim to Uhuru Peak. The sunrise above the clouds, on the way to the summit, is the moment many climbers remember most from the whole journey.

The cold is part of this night. At the summit the night temperature usually drops to between minus 10 and minus 20°C, and the wind makes it feel colder. Reaching the summit is only half the task: afterwards you descend back to Barafu Camp for lunch and continue to Mweka Camp, 3,100 m. On that day you descend almost 2,800 metres, so strong knees and trekking poles make a big difference.

content.value: Acclimatisation: altitude is the real challenge

The main risk on Kilimanjaro is not technical but physiological. At the altitude of the summit every breath holds about half the oxygen it holds at sea level, and the body needs time to adapt. Altitude sickness usually begins with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, nausea, dizziness and unusual fatigue. When the symptoms get worse, the most effective treatment is descent.

On the mountain we work with several layers of safety. The guides carry out routine medical checks throughout the climb, the group carries satellite equipment, and the first-aid kit includes emergency oxygen cylinders. The rule is clear: in the mountains there is no promise of a summit, but there is always a commitment to safety above all. Anyone whom the altitude does not allow to continue safely descends accompanied by the crew.

There is also a part for you to play: walk slowly from the very first morning, drink a lot, eat even when you have no appetite and tell the guides about any symptom. About medication that helps with altitude, consult a doctor at a travel clinic before you go.
How hard it is, and who it suits

We rate the Kilimanjaro climb as moderate in difficulty. There is no technical climbing, and no ropes or crampons are needed. What it requires is endurance: walking days of several hours in a row, cold nights in a tent and a summit day of 13 to 15 hours.

Previous climbing experience is not a requirement. If you can walk about 20 km a day, or about eight hours in a row, enjoy a challenge and come highly motivated, the climb can suit you. The minimum age in the park is 10, and there is no maximum age: climbers aged 60 and over have stood on the summit with us. A medical clearance and a health declaration are required from every participant as a condition of departure, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join.

The most important preparation is aerobic: long walks, light running or cycling, for about three months before departure. Before the flight you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call, so you reach the mountain prepared and already knowing each other.

Good to know: the climb is led by professional local guides from Tanzania who speak English and have long experience leading groups on the mountain. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory, and the route may change according to the weather and the judgement of the guides.
When to climb Kilimanjaro

Kilimanjaro lies close to the equator, so its seasons are set mainly by rain rather than by temperature. It has two rainy seasons: the long rains, roughly from March to May, and the short rains in November. In these seasons the trails are muddy, visibility is lower and the climb is harder.

The preferred seasons are January to February and June to October, the drier and more stable months, and these are when our expeditions depart. In July and August the mountain is busier with climbers. In every season the summit is very cold at night, so warm gear is always needed.
Park fees

Every climber pays Kilimanjaro National Park several fees: a conservation fee for each day in the park, a camping fee for each night, and a one-time rescue fee. The conservation fee is 70 US dollars per person per day and the camping fee 50 dollars per person per night, before VAT (as of 2026). On a seven-day climb the fees add up to several hundred dollars per person, so it is always worth checking whether they are included in the price you are offered.
On our expedition the park entry and climbing permits are included in the price, and there is nothing to pay at the gate.
Visa, vaccinations and money
Visa for Tanzania

Most visitors, including citizens of the UK, the EU and the US, need a visa to enter Tanzania. You apply in advance on the official eVisa website of the Tanzanian immigration department, and it is worth doing so several weeks before the flight. For most nationalities the visa costs 50 US dollars (100 dollars for US citizens) and it is not included in the price of the expedition. We set out the whole process, step by step, in a separate guide.
Vaccinations and health

Book an appointment at a travel clinic 4 to 6 weeks before the flight, to get personal advice on vaccinations, malaria prevention and altitude medication. There are no mosquitoes on the mountain itself, but in the lower areas, and especially on safari, the question is relevant. A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required on entry to Tanzania only in certain cases, for example after a long flight connection through a country where the disease is present, so show the doctor your full flight route.
Money and tips

The local currency is the Tanzanian shilling, but for anything related to tourism the dollar is widely accepted. The largest expense you need to bring cash for is the tips for the climbing crew, the guides, the kitchen team and the porters, which on our expedition come to 350 dollars per person. Beyond that, bring cash for personal expenses and do not rely on finding ATMs along the way. One more expense worth knowing about is the local government insurance, 44 dollars per person, which is mandatory for foreign visitors to Tanzania and does not replace travel insurance (as of 2026).
Life on the mountain

On the mountain you sleep six nights in double tents with mattresses, and before and after the climb you stay at a four-star hotel in Moshi. On the mountain you eat three full meals a day, and dinner is eaten together in a shared tent. A kitchen crew and waiters cook and serve, porters carry the logistical equipment and your personal bag, up to 15 kg per person, and you walk with a daypack only. The group has private portable toilets, and during the climb families at home receive WhatsApp updates.

The local crew is part of the experience. On the morning you leave for the gate you meet them at a celebration with dancing, and at Mweka Gate, at the end of the descent, everyone poses together for a photo, raises a toast and thanks the crew for their hard work throughout the journey.

content.value: What it costs and what is included

The price of the Kilimanjaro expedition is 2,900 US dollars per person. It includes airport transfers to Moshi and back and the transfers to the park, 2 nights in a 4-star hotel in Moshi with breakfast, 6 nights in double tents with mattresses, 3 full meals a day throughout the climb, professional local English-speaking guides, porters for personal gear, up to 15 kg per person, and for the logistical equipment, a kitchen crew and waiters, private portable toilets for the group, park entry and climbing permits, a first-aid kit with emergency oxygen cylinders, WhatsApp updates for families, a personal area in the HighAir app, a personal gear checklist with an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide, pre-departure support with flight and travel insurance questions, and a gift kit with a cap and a dry-fit shirt.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance, lunch and dinner at the hotel in Moshi, personal gear, the Tanzania visa, the local government insurance, tips for the climbing crew, and vaccinations and travel clinic advice. An extra hotel night, if needed, costs 60 dollars per person in a twin room. You can add a single room at the hotel for 90 dollars a night, a single tent for 100 dollars for the whole climb, or a roomy three-person tent you can stand up in for 150 dollars for the whole climb.

Note that in the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the climber. Before buying insurance, make sure the policy covers trekking to 5,895 m, including helicopter rescue.
Safari after the summit

Anyone who wants to add another experience to the climb can continue to three days of safari, at an additional cost. On day 9 you head to Tarangire National Park, where you see large herds of elephants, lions, giraffes and zebras. On day 10 you descend into the Ngorongoro Crater, the caldera of a collapsed volcano, where lions, elephants, buffalo and rhinoceros live on the crater floor. On day 11 you visit the Hadzabe and Datoga tribes near Lake Eyasi, one of the last communities in the world living by hunting and gathering, and at midday you drive to Kilimanjaro Airport for the flight home.

The safari is in a 4x4 vehicle with an open roof, up to 6 seats, with a fridge and charging points, and with a local English-speaking safari guide. Accommodation is 2 nights in a lodge, with 3 meals a day and mineral water, and the park entry permits are included. The tip for the safari guide, 45 dollars per person, and personal expenses are not included. After a week of effort, the safari asks for no physical effort: the wildlife viewing is done from the vehicle. The safari runs alongside our Kilimanjaro groups, so you can join it as a group and share the cost of the jeep.
Kilimanjaro with HighAir

Our Kilimanjaro expedition lasts 9 days, seven of them on the mountain on the Machame Route, and it is limited to 15 participants. Expeditions depart in the January to February and June to October seasons, the price is 2,900 US dollars per person, and the success rate we publish on the mountain is 94 per cent.

For travellers who keep Shabbat and kosher we also run a separate expedition, on the Machame Route as well, with a schedule built between two Shabbatot and a kosher kitchen on the mountain. We wrote a guide of its own about it.

content.value: A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Every climber you see on the summits of the world started once, on one mountain, and for many that mountain is Kilimanjaro. If it is your mountain, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
How many days does it take to climb Kilimanjaro?

On the HighAir expedition the whole journey lasts 9 days, seven of them on the mountain, on the Machame Route: five days of ascent to Barafu Camp, 4,673 m, a summit day and a descent day. In addition there is a night at the hotel in Moshi before the climb and a night after it. Three days of safari can be added.
How hard is it to climb Kilimanjaro?

We rate the climb as moderate in difficulty. There is no technical climbing, and no ropes or crampons are needed, but it takes endurance: anyone who can walk about 20 km a day, or about eight hours in a row, has a good starting point. The real challenge is the altitude and the cold on summit night, and the success rate we publish on the mountain is 94 per cent.
When is the best time to climb Kilimanjaro?
In January and February, and from June to October, the drier and more stable months. It is best to avoid April and November, the months of heavy rain. Our expeditions depart in the preferred seasons.
How much does it cost to climb Kilimanjaro?

The price of our expedition is 2,900 US dollars per person, and it includes the park entry and climbing permits, accommodation, meals, guides and porters. The park conservation fee alone is 70 dollars per person per day, before VAT (as of 2026). Not included are flights, travel insurance, the visa, the local government insurance and tips for the crew, 350 dollars per person.
Do I need a visa and vaccinations for Tanzania?

Most visitors, including UK, EU and US citizens, need a visa for Tanzania, applied for in advance on the official eVisa website. As for vaccinations, see a travel clinic 4 to 6 weeks before the flight and show them your full flight route, because the requirement for a yellow fever certificate also depends on the transit countries.
What language do the guides speak?

The climb is led by professional local guides from Tanzania who speak English and have long experience leading groups on the mountain. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having.
